description.narrative: In order to improve peace processes and support peace initiatives, CRs Strategic Plan 20202025 aims at improving the effectiveness of peacebuilding and peace processes. CR's vision is to transform the way the world resolves violent conflict so that people work together to build peaceful and inclusive societies. The Strategic Plan sets out four goals: 1. Adaptive and alternative paths to peace: peacebuilding overcomes barriers to creating peaceful societies, 2. Connecting people and peace efforts: more coherent initiatives help prevent and reduce violent conflict, 3. Inclusion, gender and influence: excluded groups influence approaches to building peace, 4. People centered policy: international peacebuilding support puts people first.

Sida's support to Conciliation Resources (hereafter CR) is a core support for 2020 - 2023, including an extension for 2024. Sida has been a core donor to Conciliation Resources since 2004.
CR is an international non-governmental organisation (NGO) specialising in peacebuilding. Since its establishment in 1994, Conciliation Resources has been focusing on understanding conflicts, create linkages between the different groups involved, and ensure that people directly impacted by conflict take part in its resolution. CR works with over 70 partners in, for example, Georgia, Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Nigeria, Colombia, the Republic of Fiji, and Papua New Guinea. During the coming period CR's work is guided by their Strategic Plan "Building better peace" for 2020-2025. CR has a long-term and context specific approach in the contexts where they work which mean that the type of work varies between their various programmes. CR focus on connecting divided communities with a focus on inclusion of women, youth and other gorups in society. This is done at both the community level and in more or less formal peace process at a more political level, like in Ethiopia, Bougainville and Gerorgia-Abkhasia. In addition to the context specific work, CR is also doing more thematic work and comparative learning which is published in their publication series Accord. The organisation has built up these past years a special expertise in gender equality integration in peacebuilding and in the last few years the focus on the Youth, Peace and Security agenda has increased.

Sidas stöd till Conciliation Resources (härefter CR) rör kärnstöd för perioden 2020 - 2023 inklusive en förlängning för 2024. Sida har varit en kärngivare till CR sedan 2004.
CR är en internationell icke-statlig organisation (NGO) som har specialiserat sig inom fredsbyggande. Sedan etableringen 1994 har CR fokuserat på att förstå konflikter, skapa kopplingar mellan de olika berörda grupperna och se till att människor som direkt påverkas av konflikter deltar i dess lösning. CR arbetar med över 70 partners i till exempel Georgien, Etiopien, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Centralafrikanska republiken, Nigeria, Colombia, Republiken Fiji och Papua Nya Guinea. Under den kommande perioden kommer CR:s arbete styras av den strategiska planen "Att bygga bättre fred" för 2020–2025. CR har en långsiktig och kontextspecifik strategi i de sammanhang de arbetar i vilket innebär att typen av arbete varierar mellan organisationens olika program. CR fokuserar på att skapa förbindelser mellan splittrade samhällen med fokus på inkludering av kvinnor, ungdomar och andra grupper i samhället. Detta görs både på lokal nivå och i mer eller mindre formell fredsprocess på en mer politisk nivå, som i Etiopien, Bougainville och Georgien-Abchazien. Förutom det sammanhangsspecifika arbetet gör CR också mer tematiskt arbete och jämförande lärande som publiceras i deras publikationsserie Accord. Organisationen har de senaste åren byggt upp en speciell expertis inom jämställdhetsintegrering i fredsbyggande och under de senaste åren har fokuset på ungdomar, fred och säkerhetsagendan ökat.

description.narrative:
Throughout the agreement period, CR has advocated for better policies, regulations and funding which enable longterm, adaptive and creative approaches to peace. CRs research and analysis provided knowledge to understand and share what works in peacebuilding. For example, in 2022, CR produced a new Accord Spotlight on implementing peace accords sustainably, and as part of a global research programme (XEPT), CR contributed to analysing the impact of climate change on conflict in the border regions in central and West Africa to inform peacebuilding responses.
Understanding the links between the climate crisis and conflict has been a priority in many contexts during the period. In 2022, Sida provided additional funding to this area. This initiative was designed as a 21 month project supporting local responses on the intersection between climate and conflict in three contexts (the Philippines, Kashmir and the Ugandan border region), and enabling active learning in order to adapt peace practice to evolving climate conflict challenges. A learning that has come out from the pilots is that partnering with environment focused organisations is critical to advance any work at the intersection of conflict and climate change. For example, in SE Asia, CR's partnerships with the World Agroforestry organisation, the Global Alliance for a Sustainable Planet, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, seem to have been helpful for CR to guide this work. Despite the fact that CR had to terminate this initiative earlier as a consequence to the 2023 Sida budget cuts, the pilots have served as a foundation for more strategic work on the intersection conflict-climate across the organisation.
The following are Outcome Harvesting case examples provided to Sida. The give a valuable insight to CR's work over time and what its assessed contribution is.
Horn of Africa Programme - example from Ethiopia
Outcome: Ugaaso Womens Dialogue Space was invited into leadership positions in several regional policy initiatives
Change that occurred: The Somali Non-State Actors Coalition (SONSAC), Coalition for Womens Voice in the National Dialogue (CWVND), and Jigjiga City Administration (JCA) created more space for womens leadership and voices to be included in the design and implementation of policy development and implementation initiatives. In the first case, SONSAC appointed Ugaaso Womens Dialogue Space (WDS) as Chair of their Board in January 2024. In the second case, the CWVND elected Ugaaso as a member of its national steering committee in September 2023. In the third, the JCA included Ugaaso as a member of their advisory council in February 2024.
Significance: These changes enable Ugaaso to infuse womens perspectives into various initiatives undertaken by SONSAC, the CWVND and JCA. This will facilitate implementation of political and social policies that better reflect the interests of women and marginalised groups. The SONSAC and JCA changes are particularly significant given they reflect sustained changes in fundamental governance arrangements for the respective institutions and set an important precedent for womens inclusion, rather than a one-off change in individual behaviours or relationships. The increasing popularity and growing network of Ugaaso will also provide it with a platform from which to broaden its influence and advocacy efforts, thereby having a catalytic effect on womens inclusion and participation in governance and peace processes.
Contribution: These recent developments build on years of engagement by CR and its partner KasmoDev to support women from the Somalia Regional State to convene, organise and influence more effectively. In 20192020, CR and KasmoDev convened three strategic dialogues for women from across political divides to discuss barriers to womens political participation. Based on the outcomes of these discussions and a subsequent report that was finalised in 2020, CR and KasmoDev launched the first WDS in early 2021, with the first meetings bringing together members of all registered political parties, MPs, representatives of religious groups, government officials, civil society members, including victims and survivors groups, members of Jigjiga University, and women from the diaspora. This was later formalised when the WDS decided to register Ugaaso as a CSO to ensure the sustainability and continuity of their efforts in mid-2023. CR and KasmoDev have since facilitated experience-sharing visits both within Ethiopia and abroad, enabling Ugaaso members to learn from others who have experience in advocating for womens inclusion. We have also assisted Ugaaso with conducting analytical work to assess the progress made by women and the challenges they face to inform their engagement with key institutions, including those relating to this change.
South Caucasus Programme - example from Armenia/Azerbaijan
Outcome: Civil society partners in Armenia and Azerbaijan are improving collaboration and strengthening their cohesion and unity
Change that occurred: Civil society partners in Armenia and Azerbaijan more actively communicate, collaborate, deconflict plans, strategically engage each other's networks, and when useful, deliver joint activities much more more before the project started, and particularly more so than before the military campaign in 2023, catalyzed by partner events or all-consortium events that fostered mutual interest and deeper engagement.
Significance: The fact that some actors in the CR-led consortium have initiated expanded direct contacts, and have pooled thinking, energies and sometimes partnered on activities marks a major shift in the internal cohesion and unity of effort among sub-groupings within these parts of Armenian and Azerbaijani civil society. It does not involve all partners equally and emerged partially in response to CRs leadership and the engagement opportunities it structured for consortium partners that some partners acted on more than others. The increase in interaction among peacebuilding stakeholders has meant more cohesion between the strategies of actors working in different spheres of activity (especially advocacy and community work) and in different geographies.
Contribution: CR has been able to leverage its role as consortium lead and grant manager to encourage greater collaboration between consortium members from each side. CR created or supported structured opportunities within the consortium to foster mutual awareness and relationships. These included co-hosting events, hosting voluntary online dialogues, and championing development evaluation activities that provided venues for sharing information about activities and mutual learning. The dynamic resembles a virtuous cycle, where actions taken by the consortium and by some of its partner agencies created positive self-reinforcing actions. Some partner activities are undertaken that prepare the ground for other activities by other partners and there is less clear duplication of effort.
